When a person is sullen, they are in a dark, resentful mood — and instead of talking about it or expressing it openly, they go quiet, withdrawn, and gloomy. They refuse to engage, they shut down, and they make their displeasure felt through cold silence rather than words or outbursts.

Think of it as anger that has turned inward and gone silent. It is not screaming. It is not crying. It is a heavy, hostile quietness.

To be sullen, a person usually shows all three of these at once:

1. A bad mood with a resentful edge
The person is unhappy — but not just sad. There is a bitterness or sense of grievance underneath. They feel wronged, annoyed, or frustrated about something.

2. Silence and withdrawal
They stop communicating. They won't talk normally, won't smile, won't engage. If they do speak, it is in short, flat, cold responses — like "fine," "whatever," or nothing at all.

3. A visible, gloomy presence
Even though they are silent, their mood fills the room. You can feel their sullenness. Their face is dark, closed off, and unfriendly. They are physically present but emotionally shut away.
What a Sullen Person Looks Like in Real Life

Imagine a teenager who was told they cannot go to a party. They don't shout. They don't cry. Instead, they come to dinner, sit down, stare at their plate, give one-word answers to every question, and radiate unhappiness. Their whole body seems heavy and closed. That is sullen behaviour.

Or imagine a colleague who was passed over for a promotion. They walk into work the next day saying nothing, avoiding eye contact, not responding to greetings properly, sitting alone — a dark cloud hanging over them. That person is being sullen.

• After losing the game, he sat in the corner, sullen and silent, refusing to speak to anyone.
  • She gave me a sullen look and walked out of the room without a word.
  • The child was sullen for the entire car ride after being told the trip to the zoo was cancelled.
  • He answered every question in a sullen tone, short and cold, clearly still angry about the argument.
  • The students were sullen and unresponsive during the class, their eyes down and their faces closed.
How It Differs From Similar Words

This is important because several words live near "sullen" and it is easy to mix them up.

Sullen vs. Sulky
These are very close. Sulky also means going silent and withdrawn in a bad mood — but sulky has a slightly more childish or petulant quality, like pouting because you didn't get your way. A toddler who throws themselves on the floor is sulky. Sullen is a bit darker, heavier, and more intense. An adult glaring in bitter silence is sullen. You can use sulky for adults too, but it often carries a slightly mocking or dismissive tone — as if the person is being immature. Sullen feels more serious.

Sullen vs. Grumpy
A grumpy person is irritable and might snap at you, complain, or grumble out loud. They are vocal about their bad mood. A sullen person goes silent instead. Grumpy is noisy; sullen is quiet.

Sullen vs. Moody
Moody just means your moods change and fluctuate unpredictably — you could be happy one moment and sad the next. It is a general pattern over time. Sullen describes a specific mood you are in right now: that dark, withdrawn, resentful silence.

Sullen vs. Gloomy
Gloomy leans more toward sadness and hopelessness — like feeling depressed or pessimistic. Sullen has more resentment and resistance in it. A gloomy person feels like the world is dark. A sullen person feels like they have been wronged and they are not going to let anyone forget it — silently.

Sullen vs. Brooding
Brooding means thinking deeply and darkly about something — often in a quiet, serious way. A brooding person might actually look quite intense and focused. Sullen is less about deep thought and more about a resentful, hostile withdrawal. Brooding can seem mysterious or even romantic. Sullen is generally just unpleasant to be around.

Sullen is a fairly strong word. It is not a mild or gentle bad mood — it suggests a noticeable, persistent, and somewhat hostile silence. When you describe someone as sullen, you are painting a picture of someone who is clearly, visibly, and stubbornly in a dark mood. It is the kind of mood that makes others in the room feel uncomfortable or shut out.

The word is also slightly negative in judgment — calling someone sullen is not neutral. It suggests their behaviour is unpleasant and possibly unreasonable or difficult to deal with.

In more literary or descriptive writing, sullen can be used to describe things in nature — particularly things that appear dark, heavy, threatening, and joyless.

  • The sullen sky hung low and grey, threatening rain.
  • A sullen river churned slowly through the valley.
  • The fire had burned down to a sullen glow.

Here, the word transfers the human feeling of gloomy, resentful heaviness onto the natural world. A sullen sky is not cheerful and bright — it is dark, overcast, and oppressive. This use is common in literature and formal writing.
If you had to remember just one thing: sullen = a dark, resentful bad mood expressed through cold silence and withdrawal, rather than words or outbursts.
